title: Issing’s case for looking beyond a benign euro-area inflation forecast
summary: Otmar Issing considered a euro area recovery with stable prices a plausible baseline, conditional on wage moderation, supportive financing conditions and stronger external demand. His 10 January hearing focused on the European Commission’s 1999 economic review. The figures he discussed came from several sources. Most international and private-sector institutions expected activity to expand by roughly 3% a year in 2000 and 2001. The Commission projected that employment would grow by more than 1% a year under its wage assumptions, and that consumer inflation would average around 1.5% in each year. Issing’s own argument concerned what could invalidate this attractive combination and which decisions by monetary, fiscal and structural policymakers could make it more durable (section 1).

Stronger world trade supported the export outlook. Within the euro area, financing conditions favoured investment and consumption. Continued job creation could support confidence and spending. The Commission projected that unemployment by 2001 could fall towards rates last seen in the early 1990s. The employment transmission was conditional: firms would have to find extra hiring attractive at the wages being negotiated. A cyclical expansion could raise employment without solving the structural loss of skills and job prospects among people unemployed for long periods. Issing accordingly opposed treating the projected employment improvement as assured or as an outcome the central bank could target directly (sections 1 and 5).

The inflation profile was more uneven than the annual forecasts suggested. From an estimated 1.2% in 1999, inflation was expected by the Commission to rise but stay below 2% on an annual basis. The November 1999 HICP reading of 1.6% already showed the effect of higher energy costs. The annual rate in individual months might rise further into spring and exceed the projected full-year average. Generous liquidity, a weaker euro and higher import prices were the ECB’s main upside risks. Wage agreements that extrapolated the energy-led headline increase could propagate it into a second round of domestic price increases. In the other direction, deregulation of utilities might reduce consumer prices more than forecasters assumed. Issing therefore treated an early-year peak and subsequent decline as one conditional path for inflation (sections 1–2).

Forecast accuracy was a substantive part of his policy argument. From 1969 to 1997 the European Commission’s year-ahead forecasts for both real growth and consumer price inflation for the EU as a whole had been off by around one percentage point on average. Inflation had averaged 6% during that earlier period, and growth had been more volatile. The historical error therefore puts the apparent precision of a 1.5% central forecast in context without supplying an error band for the new euro area. Monetary union itself could alter the relationships used in models, while comparable cross-country series were often unavailable. Exchange rates and oil prices also entered forecasts as assumptions even when they could change materially. He specifically points readers to the Commission’s sensitivity exercise in Box 7 (section 3).

The fiscal outlook illustrated another distinction between an observed improvement and its economic cause. The Commission projected the aggregate government deficit to fall to just below 1% of GDP by 2001. On its assumptions, stronger activity and interest-rate developments accounted for most of the improvement, with little contribution from discretionary consolidation. Issing interpreted the 1998–2001 period as yielding little additional adjustment effort at euro area level. Countries without adequate buffers could find themselves exposed when growth weakened. He urged governments to use the upswing to front-load consolidation, restructure expenditure and reduce tax burdens, and considered a gradual move towards funded pensions helpful to medium-term budgets. Those were his policy preferences, rather than commitments in member states’ fiscal plans (section 4).

His remaining structural recommendations addressed competition and the productive capacity of the economy. Easing entry and administrative costs could help firms create jobs. Opening network industries could lower input costs for business and prices for consumers, with telecommunications and parts of transport further advanced than electricity and gas. Issing assigned monetary policy a supporting role: keeping inflation and expectations low could limit risk premia in financing costs and reduce the need for workers to protect purchasing power in wage negotiations. He did not quantify the size of that premium or specify the next rate change. For an investor reading the hearing at the time, negotiations over wages, the composition of the public deficit and the responsiveness of network prices were more informative tests of the baseline than whether one monthly HICP print exceeded 1.5% (sections 5–6).

questions.question: How sensitive was the disinflation after the expected early-year peak to oil, the euro and wage assumptions?
questions.detail: The hearing identifies all three channels and an offset from utilities, but supplies no joint sensitivity estimate. Start with Box 7 of the Commission review cited by Issing, then examine contemporaneous wage settlements and the HICP components exposed to regulation. A forecast driven by exchange-rate assumptions carries different risks for a rates position than one driven by domestic wage pressure.

questions.question: How much did the projected improvement in public finances depend on the upswing?
questions.detail: The Commission saw the aggregate deficit falling while discretionary consolidation contributed little. The implications for sovereign credit vary with individual countries’ debt stocks, refinancing needs and sensitivity of revenues to growth. Compare the updated national stability programmes referenced in the hearing with their output and interest-rate assumptions. That would show which budgets had the least room to absorb a cyclical disappointment.

questions.question: Would rising employment reduce long-duration unemployment or primarily absorb workers already near employment?
questions.detail: The Commission’s forecast links wage moderation to aggregate hiring. It does not show which workers would gain the new jobs. Consult labour-force surveys by unemployment duration, employment transitions and sector, alongside measures of vacancies and wage formation. The distinction matters for estimates of spare capacity and for judging whether a strong cyclical recovery could continue without broadening inflation pressure.
